newsitem.title: USA: Dow higher at midday after Greenspan remarks.
newsitem.headline: Dow higher at midday after Greenspan remarks.

text.p: The Dow Industrials were higher at midday Tuesday as investors put a positive spin on comments by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan.
The blue chip index was up 25 points at 6869, with declines leading advances by a 12-to-10 margin on volume of about 274 million shares.

The Dow had been down more than 40 points before Greenspan's Senate testimony. It also drew strength from rallies in shares of two of its major components, International Business Machines Corp and Boeing.
The 30-year Treasury bond had been trading almost a full point lower shortly after initial excerpts were reported.

"It's straight stuff he's been talking about for a while. If he's holding any cards in his hand that are different, he's not revealing them," said Matt Alexy, chief market strategist on the trading floor at Credit Suisse First Boston, of Greenspan's remarks.

Alexy noted that the Treasury would auction $23 billion of three- and six-month bills and $17.5 billion of two-year notes this afternoon. Activity was fairly quiet at the front end of the yield curve, he said.

Also bolstering the bond market around midday were comments by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin that a strong dollar was in the best interest of the U.S. and that he was not concerned about the potential effect of a strong dollar on the U.S. trade deficit. Overnight the dollar had hit a 42-month high against the Japanese yen before closing below the 118 level.

"I think it's mostly relief over Greenspan's comments though," said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at Nationsbanc Capital Markets Inc. "He talked a lot about good inflation and some possible erosion on the good news in the future, but not in a threatening way."

Kretzmer said many participants had been shorting positions as a defensive move just in case Greenspan chose to use his appearance before the Senate as a platform to issue a warnings on inflation or monetary policy.
"There was a lot of trepidation before the speech, though few players cited any specific reasons. Now many were covering short positions, Kretzmer said.

He noted that Greenspan would be back before Congress for Humphrey-Hawkins testimony in about a month and said the Fed chairman probably was saving any substantive news he wanted to deliver about the economy until then.

Also this session, Treasury announced it would sell $7.0 billion of 10-year inflation-indexed notes on January 29, to settle on February 6. Trade in the inflation-indexed notes started and Rubin said he was unsure about maturities of future such securities.
He said the securities would be sold on a regular quarterly basis and could potentially boost savings and cut borrowing costs.
The Fed, as expected, intervened in the banking system during its usual time Tuesday, injecting reserves via a round of nine-day fixed system repurchase agreements. Fed funds were at 5-15/16 percent.
Two-year notes were unchanged at 99-19/32, yielding 5.97 percent. Five-year notes were unchanged at 99-7/32, yielding 6.31 percent. Ten-year notes were up 5/32 at 99-25/32, yielding 6.53 percent.
Three-month bill rates were up one basis point to 5.03 percent. Six-month rates were up 2/32 at 5.09 percent and year bill rates were up one basis point to 5.30 percent.
